entry.title: Mocking a Circuit Breaker: 503 While Open, Then a Half-Open Recovery
entry.summary:
Quick answer: A circuit breaker is a state machine with three states: closed, open, and half-open. When the downstream dependency fails enough times, the breaker opens and the client gets a fast failure without hammering the broken service. After a cool-down it moves to half-open and lets a trial request through. To test client behavior honestly, mock the full sequence rather than a single static 503, because the interesting logic is how the client recovers, not just how it fails. Most breaker implementations, from Resilience4j to Polly and the Go-style hand-rolled versions, share the same model. The difference between them is mostly configuration and naming.

entry.title: Your Agent's Context Fills Up Before You Type: What to Trim First
entry.summary: Most advice about coding agents is about what you type. But by the time you type your first prompt, the agent's context window is already partly full: instruction files, memory, tool names, skill descriptions. Then every file it reads, every test run and every long log adds more, and all of it is re-sent with every request. That matters for more than your bill. In Effective context engineering for AI agents, Anthropic describes context rot: as the number of tokens in the window grows, the model's ability to accurately recall information from it goes down. Their framing is that a model has an "attention budget", and every token you add spends some of it. The guiding principle they give is to "find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome." …

entry.title: How do you stop bots from deciding "Vim vs Emacs"? Building a one-human-one-vote poll
entry.summary:
Every "which tool is better" poll on the internet has the same problem: the result says more about who brought the most bots and alt accounts than about what people actually use. So I built Pollreal: 2–4 candidates, 24 hours, and every vote is one verified human. Phone once, passkey every time. You verify a phone number once (only a one-way hash is stored). After that, every vote is signed with a passkey on your own device — fingerprint, face or screen lock. One vote per device, and VPN / data-centre traffic is refused. No bandwagon. While a poll is open, only people who already voted see the split. After 24 hours the result is public, with an age and gender breakdown (small groups hidden). Each candidate gets an AI-written card that summarises the maker's official pages, with links to the sources. Results are drawn as one bar — like a fighting-game health bar — so you can see how close it was. A ranking per category using the Bradley–Terry model (the method behind Chatbot Arena), with 95% ranges: pollreal.com/rank
Open questions
I wrote down what's in place and what I haven't settled — brigades vs. real fans, bandwagon effects, the ranking method: FAIRNESS.md. I'd love for people to poke holes in it. Closed polls so far include VS Code vs Vim vs Neovim vs Emacs and PostgreSQL vs MySQL vs MongoDB vs SQLite. Results can be read without signing up.
